On your first day somebody will hand you two pages of rules, and I want to be honest with you about them. Read them, follow them, and then understand that they are not what anyone will judge you on. Nobody has ever been asked to leave a studio for forgetting a lanyard. People are asked to leave for three other things, and none of them are printed anywhere. The first is talking during playback. The second is discovering a problem at nine in the morning and mentioning it at six in the evening, when it costs four times as much to solve. And the third, which is the one that surprises people, is being right in the wrong tone of voice. You can be the most technically correct person in the room and still be the reason the session slowed down. So here is the only rule I would put on the wall: if you have to choose between being right and being useful, be useful first, and be right about thirty seconds later.

I want to talk about the word deadline, because in this industry it means two completely different things and nobody separates them out loud. There are dates that exist because of physics or because of a contract. The show goes out on Sunday at nine. The broadcaster has the slot. Nothing you do on Saturday night changes that, and if you miss it there is no show. That is a real deadline, and you must treat it as one. And then there are dates that exist because somebody wanted a comfortable margin, which is a perfectly reasonable thing to want, but it is not the same thing at all. I spent the first four years of my career treating both kinds identically, and I stayed until four in the morning more times than I want to count for dates that moved the following week without anybody telling me. So now I ask one question, early, and in a friendly voice: is this date fixed, or is this date a preference? Nobody has ever been offended by that question. Several people have been embarrassed by it, which is a different thing, and usually useful.

Pedro explains that the printed rules are the easy ones: you must wear the pass and you must not bring food into the control room. He says the rules that matter are unwritten, and that nobody tells you what they are. He gives the first one: you should not cut in while somebody is listening back to a take. He gives the second one: you should flag a problem early, in one sentence. He adds that if you are going to be late you have to send a heads-up before you are late, not after. Then he asks the other person what the unwritten rules are where they work.
